title: Orbital motion, natural and artificial satellites

notes.definition: Gravity provides the force that allows planets and satellites, both natural and artificial, to maintain circular orbits. In a circular orbit the speed is constant but the velocity is always changing, because the direction of motion keeps changing.
explanation: Planets orbit the Sun, moons orbit planets, and artificial satellites orbit the Earth. In each case, gravity provides the force that keeps the object in orbit. The force of gravity on the orbiting object always acts towards the centre of the orbit (towards the Sun or planet). Many orbits are close to circular. The orbits of planets are actually slightly elliptical, but at GCSE they are treated as circular.

Planets, moons and artificial satellites have many similarities: they all orbit a larger body, they are all kept in orbit by gravity, and they all follow close to circular paths. There are also differences. Planets orbit a star (the Sun); natural satellites (moons) orbit planets; artificial satellites are made by people and launched into orbit around the Earth (or other bodies) for purposes such as communications, weather monitoring, navigation (GPS) and observing the Earth or space.

Speed is a scalar: it only has size. Velocity is a vector: it has size and direction. An object moving in a circle at a constant speed is continuously changing direction, so its velocity is continuously changing. A changing velocity means the object is accelerating, and by Newton's first and second laws there must be a resultant force. For an orbit, this resultant force is gravity, acting towards the centre of the circle.

Because the gravitational force acts at right angles to the direction of motion, it changes the direction of the velocity but not the speed. No work is done in the direction of motion, so the object neither speeds up nor slows down. Without gravity, the object would continue in a straight line along the tangent to the circle.

For a stable orbit, the radius of the orbit must change if the speed changes. The closer an object is to the planet or star, the stronger the gravitational force on it, so it must move faster to stay in orbit at that distance. Objects in smaller orbits travel faster; objects in larger orbits travel more slowly. For example, the International Space Station, in a low orbit, travels at about 7.7 km/s, while the Moon, much further away, travels at about 1 km/s.
keyFacts: Gravity provides the force that keeps planets, moons and satellites in orbit.
The gravitational force acts towards the centre of the orbit.
Planets orbit stars; moons (natural satellites) orbit planets; artificial satellites are launched by people.
Velocity is a vector; speed is a scalar.
In a circular orbit the speed is constant but the velocity changes (direction changes).
A changing velocity is an acceleration, so there must be a resultant force: gravity.
Gravity acts at right angles to the motion, so it changes direction but not speed.
Smaller orbit radius: stronger gravity, so a higher speed is needed.
If the speed of a satellite in a stable orbit changes, the radius must change.

keyTerms.definition: The curved path of an object around a planet or star, held by gravity.
A natural body, such as a moon, that orbits a planet.
A human-made object put into orbit, for example for communications, weather or GPS.
Speed in a given direction (a vector).
How fast something is moving, with no direction (a scalar).
Towards the centre of the circle; the direction in which gravity acts on an orbiting object.

equations.name: Speed (for one orbit)
equations.formula: speed = distance ÷ time; for a circular orbit, distance = circumference = 2 × π × radius
equations.units: v in m/s, r in metres (m), T (time for one orbit) in seconds (s)

workedExamples.title: Orbital speed of the ISS
workedExamples.question: The International Space Station orbits at a radius of 6.8 × 10^6 m and takes 92 minutes to complete one orbit. Calculate its orbital speed.
steps: Distance for one orbit = 2πr = 2 × π × 6.8 × 10^6 = 4.27 × 10^7 m.

workedExamples.title: Orbital speed of the Moon
workedExamples.question: The Moon orbits the Earth at a radius of 3.84 × 10^8 m and takes 27.3 days. Calculate its orbital speed.
workedExamples.answer: About 1000 m/s (1.0 km/s): much slower than the ISS because its orbit is much larger.

workedExamples.title: Explaining constant speed but changing velocity
workedExamples.question: A satellite moves in a circular orbit at a constant speed. Explain why it is accelerating.
steps: Its direction of motion is always changing.
Velocity includes direction, so its velocity is changing.
A change in velocity is an acceleration, caused by gravity towards the centre.
workedExamples.answer: It accelerates because its velocity (direction) changes, even though its speed is constant.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think there is no gravity acting on astronauts in orbit.
misconceptions.right: In fact gravity is still strong in low orbit; it is gravity that keeps the spacecraft (and astronauts) in orbit.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think an object in a circular orbit at constant speed is not accelerating.
misconceptions.right: In fact its direction keeps changing, so its velocity changes and it is accelerating towards the centre.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think a satellite needs a force pushing it forwards to keep it moving.
misconceptions.right: In fact no forward force is needed; the only force is gravity towards the centre, which changes the direction of motion.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think satellites further away must move faster because they travel further.
misconceptions.right: In fact satellites in larger orbits move more slowly, because gravity is weaker there.

realWorld: Geostationary communication satellites orbit once every 24 hours above the equator, so they stay above the same point on Earth.
GPS satellites orbit the Earth and send signals used for navigation by phones and cars.
Weather satellites in low polar orbits scan the whole surface of the Earth as it rotates beneath them.
The International Space Station orbits about 400 km above the surface at roughly 7.7 km/s.
higherTier: Explain qualitatively how, for circular orbits, the force of gravity can lead to changing velocity but unchanged speed.
Explain qualitatively how, for a stable orbit, the radius must change if the speed changes.
separateOnlyContent: This whole subtopic is in separate Physics (8463) only, not Combined Science.
Gravity provides the force for circular orbits; compare planets, moons and artificial satellites.
examTips: When asked why velocity changes but speed does not, say: direction changes, velocity is a vector, gravity acts at right angles to the motion.
Always state that gravity acts towards the centre of the orbit (towards the planet or star).
Link orbit radius and speed: closer orbit, stronger gravity, faster speed.
For orbit calculations, use distance = 2πr and convert the time for one orbit into seconds.
summary: Gravity keeps planets, moons and artificial satellites in orbit.
Gravity acts towards the centre of a circular orbit.
Constant speed but changing velocity in a circular orbit.
Gravity at right angles to motion changes direction only.
Smaller orbits need higher speeds; changing speed changes the radius.

questions.question: Which statement about a planet orbiting the Sun is correct?
options: Its speed and velocity are both constant
Its velocity is constant but its speed changes
Its speed is constant but its velocity changes
It has no resultant force on it
markScheme: 1 mark: Its speed is constant but its velocity changes
questions.explanation: In a circular orbit the direction keeps changing, so velocity changes while speed stays constant. Gravity is the resultant force.

questions.question:
Table 1 shows the orbit radius of three objects that orbit the Earth.
Which object moves at the highest speed?
options: They all move at the same speed
One in a low orbit close to the Earth
markScheme: 1 mark: One in a low orbit close to the Earth
questions.explanation: The closer the orbit, the stronger the gravitational force, so a satellite in a low orbit must travel fastest.

questions.question: What is the same for planets, moons and artificial satellites?
options: They all orbit the Sun directly
They are all kept in orbit by gravity
They are all made by humans
They all produce their own light
markScheme: 1 mark: They are all kept in orbit by gravity
questions.explanation: All orbiting bodies are kept in orbit by gravity. Only planets orbit the Sun directly, and only artificial satellites are human-made.

questions.question: Why does the gravitational force on a satellite in a circular orbit not change its speed?
options: Gravity is too weak in space
The force acts in the direction of motion
The force acts at right angles to the direction of motion
The satellite has no mass in orbit
markScheme: 1 mark: The force acts at right angles to the direction of motion
questions.explanation: A force at right angles to the motion changes only the direction. It does no work in the direction of motion, so the speed stays the same.

questions.question: A satellite in a stable circular orbit is made to travel faster. To remain in a stable circular orbit, what must happen?
options: Its orbit radius stays the same
markScheme: 1 mark: Its orbit radius must decrease
questions.explanation: A higher speed requires a stronger gravitational force to keep it in a circle, which is only found closer to the Earth, so the radius must decrease.

questions.question: State the difference between a natural satellite and an artificial satellite.
markScheme: 1 mark: a natural satellite (moon) occurs naturally, an artificial satellite is made by people and launched into orbit
questions.explanation: Both orbit a larger body under gravity.

questions.question: Explain why speed is a scalar but velocity is a vector.
markScheme: 1 mark: speed has size (magnitude) only
1 mark: velocity has size and direction
questions.explanation: This is why an orbiting object can have a constant speed but a changing velocity.

questions.question: Compare the motion of the Moon around the Earth with the motion of the Earth around the Sun.
markScheme: 1 mark: both follow (nearly) circular orbits kept by gravity
1 mark: the Moon orbits a planet (the Earth), while the Earth orbits a star (the Sun)
questions.explanation: The same force, gravity, controls both orbits.

questions.question: Explain how the force of gravity causes a satellite in a circular orbit to have a changing velocity but a constant speed.
markScheme: 1 mark: gravity acts towards the centre of the orbit, at right angles to the direction of motion
1 mark: so it changes the direction of motion but not the speed
1 mark: velocity includes direction, so the velocity changes (the satellite accelerates) while the speed stays constant
questions.explanation: A perpendicular force changes direction only.

questions.question: Explain why satellites in low orbits must travel faster than satellites in high orbits.
markScheme: 1 mark: closer to the Earth the gravitational force is stronger
1 mark: so a higher speed is needed to stay in a stable orbit (rather than falling inwards)
questions.explanation: The radius and speed of a stable orbit are linked: smaller radius, higher speed.

questions.question: Name the force that provides the resultant force on a planet orbiting the Sun.
markScheme: 1 mark: gravity (gravitational attraction of the Sun)
questions.explanation: Gravity is the only significant force on the orbiting planet.

questions.question: A satellite's orbit gradually loses speed because of a thin atmosphere. Suggest and explain what happens to its orbit.
markScheme: 1 mark: its orbit radius decreases (it moves closer to the Earth)
1 mark: because for a stable orbit the radius must change when the speed changes; at its lower speed gravity pulls it inwards
questions.explanation: Losing speed means gravity is more than enough to keep it in its current circle, so it moves inwards to a smaller orbit. Over time, this makes the satellite fall back into the atmosphere.

questions.question: Explain why a satellite in a circular orbit is accelerating, even though its speed is constant.
markScheme: 1 mark: its direction of motion is continuously changing, so its velocity is changing
1 mark: acceleration is a change in velocity, so it is accelerating (towards the centre)
questions.explanation: Acceleration is about velocity, which includes direction.
